propositions.text: The claimant and his spouse, Venezuelan citizens, seek refugee protection under sections 96 and 97(1) of IRPA.
propositions.quote: XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX (herein "the claimant"), and his spouse, XXXXXXXXXX XXXXXX, both citizens of Venezuela,1 seek refugee protection pursuant to sections 96 and 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act2 (the IRPA).

paragraphs.summary: The claimant and spouse, Venezuelan citizens, seek refugee protection under IRPA sections 96 and 97(1).

propositions.text: The claimant alleges a 2007 car incident hitting a man identifying as a police officer who later extorted him for $20,000 USD.
propositions.quote: The claimant alleges that he was involved in a car incident on XXXXXX, 2007 at X o'clock in the morning whereby he hit a man who identified himself as a police officer.

propositions.text: The claimant called emergency, police and ambulance arrived 30 minutes later; he gave a declaration and his car was retained then released by court order.
propositions.quote: He called the emergency from his cell phone and the ambulance and police arrived 30 minutes later. He followed the police to the Transit Department (Instituto Nacional de Transito y Transporte Terreste - INTTT), where he provided a declaration. He spent most of the day at the INTTT and his car was retained for further investigation. Two weeks later, his lawyer got a court order to have his car released.

propositions.text: The injured man, XXX, demanded $20,000 USD; the claimant reported extortion to his lawyer who said legal action was impossible due to circumstances.
propositions.quote: Two weeks later, the man he had injured, a Mr. XXXXXXXXX (herein referred to as "XXX") called him, demanding $35,000,000 Boliveres pesos ($U.S.20,000) for the injuries he suffered. He went to see his lawyer, Mr. XXXXXXXX XXXXXXX, (herein referred to as "XXX") to report the extortion. He was advised that legally XXX was unable to do anything to him in court due to the impossibility of the claimant having been able to see XXX on the roadway due to the hour and the curve in the road.

propositions.text: The claimant states legal action was impossible despite two years and all influences of XXX.
propositions.quote: The claimant states in his narrative that "they have been unable to take legal action against me, even though two years have passed and all of their influences."

paragraphs.summary: The claimant alleges a 2007 car incident hitting a police officer who extorted him; legal action was impossible despite two years and influences, per claimant.

propositions.text: XXX called claimant multiple times daily, forcing claimant to report extortion and threats to police at CICPC in 2007.
propositions.quote: XXX would call the claimant at his house sometimes two or five times per day, so the claimant states that he had no choice but to go to the police to report the extortion and threats.

propositions.text: Claimant reported extortion and threats to police at CICPC on XXXXXXXX, 2007; police said they would investigate.
propositions.quote: He states in his narrative that he did so on XXXXXXXX, 2007 at the police department called Centro de Investigciones Cientificas Penales y Crimnaliisticas (CICPC). The police told him they would investigate.

paragraphs.summary: The claimant alleges XXX called him multiple times daily, leading him to report extortion and threats to police at CICPC in 2007.

propositions.text: In 2008, claimant was attacked by XXX and others identifying as police; attackers fled after wife's screams.
propositions.quote: On XXXXXX, 2008 the claimant and his wife were arriving home when the claimant was attacked by XXX and others who identified themselves as police officers. Due to his wife's screaming, the attackers fled in a XXXXXXXXXXXX with no license plates.

propositions.text: Claimant sought medical attention and reported attack to police (CICPC) next day; moved to new address and changed phone numbers on lawyer's advice.
propositions.quote: The claimant sought medical attention at a clinic and reported the incident the next day to police (CICPC). After this he took his lawyer's advice and moved to another address in his city and changed his phone numbers, including his cell.

propositions.text: XXX continued threatening claimant and wife by phone; they reported again to police and moved to another city on lawyer's advice.
propositions.quote: However, XXX continued to call him at his new address and on his work cell frequently (three to five times per day) threatening to kill him. In XXX 2008, XXX called again, telling him that he knew where he worked and lived and that he would not escape death. He also called the claimant's wife and threatened to kill her also. They reported to the police again to make a denunciation. Once again, the police officer took their report and told them they would investigate. The claimant took his lawyer's advice and moved outside of XXXXX to the city of XXXXX, some 1 1/2 hours away.

paragraphs.summary: In 2008, claimant was attacked by XXX and others; after reporting and threats, he and wife moved cities on lawyer's advice.

propositions.text: In 2008, claimant was shot at by XXX; he reported to police, gave bullets, and lawyer advised him to leave Venezuela.
propositions.quote: He states that he saw XXX on the other side of the fence with another person. XXX immediately took a 9mm pistol and fired at the claimant a few times. Luckily the claimant was not harmed and he was able to recover the two bullets. He testified he reported to the police in XXXXX, however they told him to report to the police in XXXXX. He drove there, reporting to police and also gave them the bullets.4 He called his lawyer who became very concerned that the police did nothing to protect the claimant so he advised him to leave Venezuela.

propositions.text: Claimant left Venezuela for Canada in 2008 and claimed protection six months later in 2009.
propositions.quote: The claimant immediately called his friend in Canada who offered him a place to stay. They left Venezuela on XXXXXXX, 2008 and claimed protection XX months later on June 2, 2009.

paragraphs.summary: Claimant was shot at in 2008, reported to police, lawyer advised leaving Venezuela; claimant left for Canada and claimed protection in 2009.

propositions.text: Claimants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection.
propositions.quote: I find the claimants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the claimants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection.

propositions.text: There are issues of credibility within the claimant's claim after reviewing testimony and written evidence.
propositions.quote: Having reviewed the written and oral testimony of the claimant, I find there are issues of credibility within this claim.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds credibility issues in the claimant's claim after reviewing evidence and testimony.

propositions.text: Claimant's narrative indicates he hit a police officer in 2007 who tried to extort money, a common occurrence in Venezuela.
propositions.quote: The claimant's narrative and oral testimony indicated that he was involved in an incident on XXXXXX, 2007 in which he struck a police officer named XXX who he believed had set up the accident in efforts to extort money from him. The claimant's explanation was that this was something quite common in Venezuela.

paragraphs.summary: The claimant's narrative indicates a 2007 incident hitting a police officer who tried to extort money, common in Venezuela.

propositions.text: Police reports state the incident with XXX occurred in 2005, conflicting with claimant's 2007 date in PIF and testimony.
propositions.quote: Upon closer review of the police reports filed by the claimant, I note two reports in which the claimant has stated that the incident with XXX occurred in 2005.

propositions.text: Two police reports from 2007 and 2008 state the initial incident with XXX happened in 2005.
propositions.quote: Clearly the dates in these two reports filed in XXXXXX 2007 and XXXXX 2008 refer to the initial incident with XXX as happening in 2005.

propositions.text: The inconsistency in dates was not addressed at hearing; claimant's lawyer's statement lacks weight due to lack of notarization and signature.
propositions.quote: This inconsistency was not noticed at the hearing and therefore the claimant was not asked to explain the discrepancy... I am unable to assign much weight to this statement as it is not notarized, has no date on it nor do I find his name or signature on any of the police reports or any witness statements made by him to police regarding the XXXXX 2007 incident which he states he was present at the scene two hours after it happened.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds police reports date incident to 2005, conflicting with claimant's 2007 date; lawyer's statement lacks weight.

propositions.text: Claimant traveled to Panama and Miami in 2007 around the time of the incident with XXX.
propositions.quote: At the hearing, however, questions were put to the claimant regarding his travel outside of Venezuela. For example the claimant departed Venezuela for Panama on XXXXXXXX, 2007, returning from that visit on XXXXXXXX, 2007. He then left for a business trip to Miami on XXXXXX, 2007 and returned the same day. According to his evidence, the initial encounter and incident with XXX happened the following day on XXXXXX, 2007.

propositions.text: Claimant said he returned to Venezuela for work despite extortion threats, but PIF indicated the trip was as a visitor.
propositions.quote: The claimant was asked why he returned to Venezuela if he was being extorted and threatened by XXX. The claimant responded, "I went there for work and up to that point in time, there had been no attempts to kill me." I note however the claimant's PIF indicated that this trip was that of a visitor.

paragraphs.summary: Court notes claimant traveled to Panama and Miami in 2007 near incident date; claimant said return was for work but PIF says visitor.

propositions.text: Claimant's returns to Venezuela in 2007 and 2008 contradict claimed fear of persecution or death threats.
propositions.quote: I find that the claimant's travel to and re-availment to Venezuela on XXXXXXX, 2007 is inconsistent with his alleged fear of persecution or a threat to his life at the hands of XXX...

propositions.text: Claimant's return from Miami in 2008 despite prior attack and threats shows lack of subjective fear until shooting incident in 2008.
propositions.quote: Similarly, I find the claimant's return from a 10-day business trip to Miami, from XXXXXX to XXXXXX 2008, is indicative of a lack of subjective fear given his having been beaten by XXX on XXXXXX, 2008... I conclude that he did not possess a subjective fear until that incident on XXXXXX, 2008.

propositions.text: Claimant's explanation for returning to Venezuela despite death threats is not credible; leaving wife behind also not credible.
propositions.quote: I am unable to assign any weight to the claimant's explanation when asked the reasons for returning to Venezuela on XXXXXX, 2008 given that he had, according to statements made in his narrative, been threatened with death by XXX... I find it not credible that the claimant would leave his wife in XXXX to travel to the United States if he believed XXX's threat...

paragraphs.summary: Court finds claimant's returns to Venezuela despite threats show lack of subjective fear until 2008 shooting; explanations not credible.

propositions.text: Claimant and wife moved to XXXX in 2008 and changed jobs; claimant worked for relative's company and then another employer before leaving Venezuela.
propositions.quote: The claimant's testimony and evidence indicates that he and his wife moved to XXXX in XXX 2008 and also changed their jobs... The claimant took on a job as XXXXXXXXXX of a company in XXXX from XXXX 2008 to XXXXX, 2008, which he indicated was a business owned by a relative... He then returned to XXXXXXXXXXXXX for a company called XXXXXXXXXXXXXX on XXXXX, 2008.

propositions.text: Claimant stopped working the day before departure and did not notify employer until after arriving in Canada.
propositions.quote: His last date of work with this company was XXXXXXX, 2008, the day before his departure, however he explained that he did not notify the company until after he arrived in Canada.

paragraphs.summary: Claimant and wife moved and changed jobs in 2008; claimant stopped work day before departure and notified employer after arriving in Canada.

propositions.text: Claimant's delay in leaving Venezuela until 2008 undermines credibility and subjective fear of persecution.
propositions.quote: I find, had the claimant possessed a well-founded fear of persecution, he would have not returned to Venezuela after his trips abroad... I find that the claimant's delay in departing Venezuela until XXXXXX 2008 impugns his credibility.

propositions.text: Delay in making refugee claim is relevant to credibility and subjective fear but not usually decisive alone.
propositions.quote: Delay has been recognized by the Federal Court as an important factor in assessing a claimant's credibility and their subjective fear... While delay in making a refugee claim is not in itself usually decisive, it is a relevant factor to be considered when assessing the overall viability of the claim.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds claimant's delay in leaving Venezuela undermines credibility; delay is relevant but not usually decisive in refugee claims.

propositions.text: Claimant lacked subjective fear as shown by repeated returns to city of threats and no contact with XXX between 2008 moves and shooting incident.
propositions.quote: I find that the claimant did not possess a subjective fear particularly given his testimony that he had no further contact with XXX between XXXX 2008 and the shooting incident of XXXXXX, 2008.

propositions.text: Claimant's actions of returning from trips abroad in 2008 corroborate lack of subjective fear.
propositions.quote: This lack of fear is corroborated by the claimant's own actions of returning from a trip abroad as late as XXXXXX 2008.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds claimant lacked subjective fear due to no contact with XXX and returning from trips abroad in 2008.

propositions.text: It is implausible police in XXXX would not investigate the 2008 attempted murder incident; police told claimant to report elsewhere, which does not make sense.
propositions.quote: I am unable to find plausible that the police in XXXX would not take a report or investigate the XXXXXX, 2008 incident regarding the attempted murder of the claimant by XXX... I find that this does not make any sense because it would provide evidence that XXX had traveled to XXXX for the purpose of an attempted murder...

propositions.text: The 2008 police report about the shooting incident is in evidence and will be discussed under state protection.
propositions.quote: Notwithstanding, the XXXXXX, 2008 police report has been filed into evidence and more about this shall be discussed below under state protection.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds police refusal to investigate 2008 shooting implausible; report is in evidence and discussed under state protection.

propositions.text: Claimant's failure to seek asylum in US or Panama despite visits undermines credibility of fear of persecution.
propositions.quote: In addition, given the claimant's visits for work or otherwise to Panama, Miami or Los Angeles, I find that his not having sought asylum in the United States or Panama undermines the credibility of his alleged fear of persecution.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds claimant's failure to seek asylum in US or Panama despite visits undermines credibility of fear.

propositions.text: Claimant delayed six months after arriving in Canada to claim protection; explanation about needing corroboration lacks weight.
propositions.quote: The claimant delayed making his claim for protection for six months after arriving in Canada. His explanation was that he believed that he had to support his claim with corroborative evidence. I am unable to assign any weight to this explanation...

propositions.text: Claimant had a friend in Canada who invited him in 2005, per CIC notes.
propositions.quote: ...given the claimant's testimony that he had a friend living in Canada who it would appear from CIC notes, was the same friend who had invited him to Canada in 2005...

paragraphs.summary: Court finds claimant delayed six months to claim protection; explanation lacks weight; friend invited him to Canada in 2005.

propositions.text: Claimant and wife were denied Canadian visas in 2005 due to employment letter and bonafide visitor concerns; later granted visas after reapplication.
propositions.quote: I note that the claimant and his wife were denied in their applications for Canadian visas in 2005... Subsequent notes on the CIC file indicate that the claimants reapplied and were granted Canadian visas...

propositions.text: The 2005 visa denial coincides with police reports stating initial incident with XXX occurred in 2005.
propositions.quote: ...it is coincidental that the claimants' first attempt to leave Venezuela for whatever purpose was soon after the date as it stated by the claimant in statements made by him in the XXXXXX 2007 and XXXXXX 2008 reports, which was XXXXXX, 2005.

paragraphs.summary: Court notes 2005 Canadian visa denial coincides with police reports of initial incident in 2005.

propositions.text: Despite credibility concerns, the key issue is state protection, not just credibility or delay.
propositions.quote: Irrespective of my credibility concerns... the determinative issue, even were I not to have credibility concerns, is that of state protection.

paragraphs.summary: Court states that despite credibility concerns, the key issue is state protection.

propositions.text: Claimant's repeated returns to Venezuela before 2008 show no subjective fear; delay in leaving after shooting inconsistent with fear.
propositions.quote: I have found that the claimant re-availed to Venezuela numerous times prior to 2008, clearly indicating that he possessed no subjective fear... the claimants delayed leaving the country for over two weeks after having been issued Canadian visas... I again determine that this is inconsistent with a subjective fear...

propositions.text: Claimant's fear is of criminality by a rogue police officer, not persecution.
propositions.quote: I find that the circumstances of the claimant and his fear of a rogue police officer, who was attempting to extort, threaten and kill the claimant, is a fear of criminality.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds claimant had no subjective fear before 2008 and delayed leaving after shooting; fear is of criminality, not persecution.

propositions.text: Claimants fear XXX and the government due to opposition to Chavez government
propositions.quote: The claimants have stated to immigration officials that they fear XXX but also the government because they are against the Chavez government.

propositions.text: No weight assigned to claimants' statement about lack of government protection due to anti-Chavez beliefs
propositions.quote: I am unable to assign any weight to their stating that they did not receive protection from the government because of their anti-Chavez government beliefs.

propositions.text: Counsel concedes claimants fall under section 97 and state protection is the key issue
propositions.quote: counsel has conceded that the circumstances of these claimants fall under section 97 and that the determinative issue is that of state protection.

paragraphs.summary: Claimants say they fear XXX and government due to anti-Chavez views; court gives no weight to this; counsel concedes state protection is key issue under section 97.

propositions.text: Issue is whether principal claimant faces risk of death, cruel treatment, or torture if returned to Venezuela
propositions.quote: The next issue in this case is whether the principal claimant would, on a balance of probabilities, be subjected to a risk to his life, or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, or a danger of torture, if he were to return to Venezuela.

paragraphs.summary: Court states issue is whether claimant faces risk of death, cruel treatment, or torture if returned to Venezuela.

propositions.text: Presumption that state can protect citizens unless state is in complete breakdown
propositions.quote: There is a presumption that the state is capable of protecting its citizens except in situations where the state is in complete breakdown.

propositions.text: Claimant must prove on balance of probabilities that state protection is inadequate
propositions.quote: A claimant, who alleges that state protection is not available, must persuade the Board that, on a balance of probabilities, the evidence establishes that state protection is inadequate.

propositions.text: Claimant can rebut presumption by clear and convincing evidence of state's inability to protect
propositions.quote: A claimant can rebut the presumption by providing clear and convincing evidence of the state's inability to protect.

propositions.text: Claimant must approach state for protection if it might reasonably be forthcoming
propositions.quote: The onus is on the claimant to approach the state for protection in situations where state protection might reasonably be forthcoming.

paragraphs.summary: Court explains presumption state can protect unless breakdown; claimant must prove inadequacy on balance of probabilities with clear evidence and seek state protection first.

propositions.text: State need not guarantee perfect protection; failure to protect all citizens is insufficient for claim
propositions.quote: No government can be expected to guarantee perfect protection of all of its citizens at all times, and the fact that a state is not always successful in protecting its citizens is not enough to justify a claim.

propositions.text: When state controls territory and has authorities making serious protection attempts, claim is less justified
propositions.quote: This is particularly true when a state is in effective control of its territory and has military, police and civil authorities in place and is making serious attempts to protect its citizens.

paragraphs.summary: Court states state need not guarantee perfect protection; effective control and serious protection efforts reduce claim justification.

propositions.text: Burden to prove lack of state protection depends on state's democracy level
propositions.quote: The burden of proving an absence of state protection is directly proportional to the level of democracy that exists in the state.

propositions.text: Documentary evidence shows Venezuela is a functioning democracy with political and judicial systems
propositions.quote: The documentary evidence before the Board indicates Venezuela is a functioning democracy.

propositions.text: Venezuela has official apparatus to provide some protection to citizens
propositions.quote: It has functioning political and judicial systems in place, and an official apparatus sufficient to provide a measure of protection to its citizens.

propositions.text: Local policing failures do not equal lack of state protection unless part of pattern of state inability or refusal
propositions.quote: Local failures to provide effective policing do not amount to a lack of state protection unless they are part of a pattern of state inability or refusal to provide protection.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds Venezuela is a functioning democracy with protection apparatus; local police failures alone don't prove lack of state protection.

propositions.text: Venezuela controls territory with functioning military and police; no total state breakdown
propositions.quote: Venezuela is in control of its territory and has functioning security forces, both military and police, in place. There is no evidence of a total breakdown of state authority in the country.

propositions.text: Heavy burden to show one should not exhaust domestic remedies when state authority intact
propositions.quote: Therefore, the burden of attempting to show that one should not be required to exhaust all avenues of domestic recourse is a heavy one.

propositions.text: Venezuelan security forces are hierarchical and allow complaints to higher authority
propositions.quote: The Venezuelan security forces are hierarchical and allow a person to complain to a higher authority if dissatisfied with the services provided.

propositions.text: National Guard and police services maintain order including in major centers
propositions.quote: The National Guard, a branch of the military that maintains order, is complemented by state and local police services, as well as city forces in the major centers such as XXXX.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds Venezuela controls territory with functioning security forces and hierarchical complaint system; heavy burden to avoid exhausting domestic remedies.

propositions.text: Claimants sought protection four times; police did not arrest XXX despite promises to investigate
propositions.quote: Counsel has submitted that the claimants sought protection on four occasions and that the police did not arrest XXX even though they said they would investigate.

propositions.text: Police in Venezuela struggle with corruption and criminality but efforts to change exist
propositions.quote: I agree with counsel that the documentary evidence currently before the Board shows that the police in Venezuela continue to struggle with issues of corruption and criminality. However, efforts to change are also shown with the documents before the Board.

propositions.text: Chavez created new National Police Force paying triple average salary, described as ethical
propositions.quote: In a recent report, Chavez created a new National Police Force, a force which pays "three times the current average police salary" and which the Justice Minister described as "...a decent body, irreproachable and ethical for which we must ensure proper conduct by officials."

paragraphs.summary: Counsel says claimants sought police protection four times; court agrees police struggle with corruption but notes reforms like new National Police Force.

propositions.text: Ministry of Interior investigating 1,800 of 9,000 police officers for misconduct
propositions.quote: Further, the Ministry of the Interior appears to be dealing with the issues of police misconduct in Venezuela and currently 1,800 of 9,000 police officers are under investigation by the Ministry.

propositions.text: 2010 Dept of State Report notes impunity problem but prosecutions of abusive police officers occur
propositions.quote: The recent Department of State Report for 2010 indicated that impunity remains a problem however police officers, who have committed abuses, are being prosecuted.

propositions.text: In 2010, over 9,610 complaints made against police; some officers arrested
propositions.quote: This report states that in 2010 there were over 9,610 complaints made against police officers and even evidence provided on behalf of the claimants indicates police officers had been arrested.

propositions.text: Claimant did not provide evidence that XXX was connected to higher officials
propositions.quote: the claimant in the circumstances of his situation has not provided any evidence to suggest that XXX was connected to any higher leveled official.

propositions.text: Claimant said all police work for government and cover each other's back
propositions.quote: When asked about this, he responded that all police work for the government and they cover each other's back.

paragraphs.summary: Ministry investigates many police officers; prosecutions occur despite impunity; claimant gave no evidence XXX linked to higher officials; claimant said police cover each other.

propositions.text: Claimant filed police reports multiple times, including last month before leaving Venezuela
propositions.quote: In the circumstances of this claim, it is clear that the claimant was not reluctant to file denunciations with the police even though he believes that they cover each other's back. He did so several times; the last time the same month as he departed Venezuela for the final time.

propositions.text: Police said little to investigate without proof or witnesses despite claimant naming XXX as perpetrator
propositions.quote: While police reports show that XXX was named by the claimant as the perpetrator of threats, beatings and the attempt against his life in XXXXXX 2008, when questioned about what the police told him, the claimant replied that the police indicated that there was little to investigate if there was no proof of who made the calls or there were no witnesses to attacks made upon him.

propositions.text: Claimants had other avenues like higher police authorities and Ministry of Interior to pursue complaints
propositions.quote: Even so, I find that, if the claimants were dissatisfied with the attention or lack service provided by police, they had other avenues to pursue such as higher levels of police authorities.

propositions.text: Claimant's lawyer reported to police and Attorney General, advised claimant to flee due to police inaction
propositions.quote: When asked about this, the claimant responded that he had a lawyer who reported to the police and the Attorney General, and his lawyer was of the opinion that the police were not doing anything and told him to flee.

propositions.text: Claimant's return to same police despite belief of inaction unreasonable but could have complained to Ministry of Interior
propositions.quote: While I can find it unreasonable that the claimant returned to the same police authorities in XXXX if he indeed believed they were not doing anything, I find that, under the circumstances, he could have complained to the Ministry of the Interior as documentation indicates they are actively investigating police misconduct in that country.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds claimant filed police reports multiple times; police said little to investigate; other complaint avenues existed; lawyer advised fleeing; claimant could have complained to Ministry.

propositions.text: Persecutor being police officer does not mean state is agent of persecution or protection unavailable
propositions.quote: The Federal Court has ruled that the fact that the persecutor was a police officer does not mean that the state itself is the agent of persecution, or that state protection is not available.

propositions.text: Claimant must seek available redress before seeking protection from another state
propositions.quote: It also does not relieve the claimant from seeking available redress before seeking protection from another state.

propositions.text: Misconduct by some police officers does not prove state's inability to protect citizens
propositions.quote: Further, the behavior of some police officers does not obviate the need to seek the protection from the authorities since that is not sufficient proof of the state's inability to protect its citizens.

paragraphs.summary: Federal Court rulings: police persecutor does not equal state persecution; claimant must seek redress first; police misconduct alone insufficient to prove lack of state protection.

propositions.text: Claimant failed to prove inadequate state protection or to pursue all reasonable protection steps
propositions.quote: I find that the claimant has not established, on a balance of probabilities, that there is inadequate state protection in Venezuela, nor has he taken all reasonable steps in the circumstances to pursue the available state protection.

propositions.text: Claimant failed to rebut presumption of state protection with clear and convincing evidence; claim fails under s. 97 IRPA
propositions.quote: I find the claimant has failed to rebut the presumption of state protection with clear and convincing evidence and the claim fails under s. 97 of the IRPA.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds claimant failed to prove inadequate state protection or pursue all steps; claim fails under section 97 IRPA.

propositions.text: Claimant's wife's claim relies on his and thus fails as well
propositions.quote: The claimant's wife relies on the claimant's claim and thus her claim fails as well.

paragraphs.summary: Court concludes claimant's wife's claim fails as it relies on his claim.

propositions.text: Claimants are not Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection; claims rejected
propositions.quote: Having given due consideration to all of the evidence before it, the relevant provisions of the IRPA, and to the jurisprudence upon which the Board relies, I find the claimants are not Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection. Accordingly, these claims for refugee protection are rejected.

paragraphs.summary: Court concludes claimants are not refugees or persons in need of protection; claims rejected.
